new_statements.rule_in_words: Arakanese (Rakhine) is a Burmese-type tone language (heavy, level/low, creaky, stop-final tones on every full syllable). The only prominence asymmetry described is full vs. reduced ('weak') syllables: reduced syllables carry a toneless schwa and occur only in non-final position (first syllable of a disyllable; first, second or both of a trisyllable), so the word-final syllable is always a full tone-bearing syllable. Neither Bradley 1985, Okell 1995 nor Ono 1970 makes any statement about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Bradley: syllables with etymological stop finals rarely reduce; full forms may surface in slow/formal speech; Arakanese reduces nasal-final syllables less than Burmese but has a few reductions Burmese lacks. Okell 1995:15-16: Arakanese uses weakening more extensively than Standard Burmese overall, yet some SB weak syllables are full in Arakanese.
new_statements.domain_note: Word defined by juncture (Sprigg 1957); statements concern lexical words/compounds in citation and connected speech. Described variety is Arakanese of the Sittwe/Mrauk-U type, not specifically the Yan-bye/Ramree (Yangbye) variety; Okell 1995:7 treats Arakanese phonemes and tones 'as for SB except as set out below'.
new_statements.identity_note: yang1301 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 [ybd] 'Yangbye' was retired in 2012 (CR 2011-043) and merged into Rakhine [rki] = rakh1245. 'Yangbye' is Ethnologue's spelling of Yan-bye (Burmese name of Ramree Island; Davis 2014:8 lists 'Yangbye (Rambree, Yanbe, Yanbye, Yangbye)' as a Rakhine dialect; Okell 1995:3 'the dialect of Kyauk-hpyu and Yan-bye (Ramree) in the centre'; Bradley 1985:181 'rambre.. around Ramree Island'). No linguistic description of the Yan-bye/Ramree variety itself exists beyond unpublished SIL survey wordlists (Yaw & Statezni 2012) and Ono's 1970 Kyaukpyu notes. The quoted statement (Bradley 1985) describes Arakanese generally from Sittwe/Mrauk-U-type speakers; Okell 1995 describes Sittwe District Arakanese. Any catalog entry belongs under rakh1245 (Rakhine), not under the retired code.

sources.note: No stress statement as such. p.190: schwa vowel 'on which there is no tonal contrast'; the word is defined by juncture (Sprigg 1957); reduced syllables occur as the first syllable of disyllables and first/second/first-two of trisyllables (never final); Arakanese reduces less than Burmese. pp.198-199: four tones (heavy, level, creaky, stop-final) realized much as in Burmese. 'accent' used only in the sense of regional accent.
sources.venue: Linguistics of the Sino-Tibetan area: the state of the art

sources.citation: Okell, John. 1995. Three Burmese dialects. In David Bradley (ed.), Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 13: Studies in Burmese languages, 1-138. Pacific Linguistics A-83. Canberra: ANU. (Arakanese = section 2, Sittwe District data)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: No use of the word stress/accent. Outline phonology (p.7) lists five 'tones': heavy, creaky, low, stop, and 'weak' (the reduced toneless syllable); 'Phonemes are as for SB except as set out below'; section 2.3.2.2 (pp.15-16): 'Weakening in AR occurs in the same way, and with the same voicing pattern, as in SB.. AR however makes more extensive use of weakening than SB' (first syllables of compounds reduced to C + schwa). Identifies Kyauk-hpyu/Yan-bye (Ramree) as the central main variety of Arakanese (p.3).
sources.venue: Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 13: Studies in Burmese languages

sources.citation: Davis, Heidi A. 2014. Consonant correspondences of Burmese, Rakhine and Marma with initial implications for historical relationships. MA thesis, University of North Dakota. xiv+135 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress (no occurrence of stress/accent in the prosodic sense); tone deliberately omitted from transcriptions. Useful for identity: p.8 lists Rakhine dialects 'Chaungtha, Kyaukphyu, Man Aung, Mrauk-U, Sittwe, and Yangbye (Rambree, Yanbe, Yanbye, Yangbye)'; cites Jarernponganarn 1997 (Mahidol MA on Sittwe Arakanese phonology) and Yaw & Statezni 2012 (unpublished SIL survey of Rakhine varieties).

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2011. Change Request Number 2011-043: merge Chaungtha [ccq] and Yangbye [ybd] into Rakhine [rki] (adopted 2012-02-03). SIL International. 5 pp.
sources.note: Nothing; states Yangbye and Chaungtha are varieties of Rakhine, wordlists from 'Yangbye island' and Kyauktaw >=94% lexically similar to Sittwe Rakhine; cites Bradley 1985, Okell 1995, Matisoff 1986.

sources.citation: Huziwara, Keisuke [藤原敬介]. 2003. マルマ語の音声に関する考察 [A phonetic analysis of Marma]. 京都大学言語学研究 (Kyoto University Linguistic Research) 22: 237-300.
sources.note: Marma (divergent Arakanese of the Chittagong Hill Tracts; separate glottocode), not Yangbye. No word-stress section; §2.5 tones (summarises D. Bernot 1958, whose tone 2 has 'strong stress at syllable onset', then author's own 4-way tone analysis); §2.6.2 vowel weakening: first element of CVCV compounds realized as Cə, CəCV being the more stable word shape.

sources.citation: Ono, Toru [大野徹]. 1970. ビルマ語方言の研究 (1) 南西方言 [Burmese dialectology 1: South-Western dialects]. 大阪外国語大学学報 (Journal of Osaka University of Foreign Studies) 22: 81-106. (In Japanese, English summary; data from Akyab-Mrohaung, Kyaukpyu, Man-Aung, Sandoway)
sources.note: No stress/accent statement (no アクセント/強勢 in text). Gives syllable structure CV/CVC, rhyme correspondences for the Kyaukpyu (チャウピュー) dialect, and states the SW dialects have a three-tone system corresponding regularly to Standard Burmese tones; classifies SW Burmese into Akyab-Mrohaung, Kyaukpyu-Ramree, Cheduba, Sandoway and Marma.
